Tables and charts

PLL adds tables to Python: you do not need to import anything to use them. A table shows up in the interactions panel as a card you can scroll, with a Save CSV button, which saves the whole table. A number is shown as Python prints it (2.0, 12999.99), and a column of numbers lines up on the right, so a column of numbers that is still text (from a CSV) stands out by lining up on the left. Each operation below is shown with its contract (the types of its inputs and output), followed by some examples and what they produce.

Tables never change: every operation on a table produces a new table, and leaves the original as it was. Operations on tables are methods, written after the table with a dot, like workouts.filter(is_long). For type annotations, the type of a table is Table, and the type of a row is dict.

A table is not a list or a dictionary: its rows and columns are taken out with its methods, row and column, and a mistake like this one says which to use: 

table(["name"], [["Ada"]])["name"]
TypeError: a table's columns are not taken out with square brackets: write t.column("name") for the values in it.

Creating tables​

table​ 

table(columns: list[str], rows: list[list]) -> Table

A table with the given column names, and the given rows, each of which is a list with one value for each column (in the same order as columns). 

workouts = table(
    ["date", "activity", "duration"],
    [
        ["2025-04-01", "Running", 30],
        ["2025-04-02", "Yoga", 45],
        ["2025-04-03", "Cycling", 60],
        ["2025-04-04", "Running", 25],
        ["2025-04-05", "Yoga", 50],
    ],
)
workouts
date activity duration
2025-04-01 Running 30
2025-04-02 Yoga 45
2025-04-03 Cycling 60
2025-04-04 Running 25
2025-04-05 Yoga 50

A row can also be a dict, like the ones t.row(n) gives you, so you can make a new table from some of the rows of another: 

table(workouts.columns(), [workouts.row(0), workouts.row(2)])
date activity duration
2025-04-01 Running 30
2025-04-03 Cycling 60

table_from_columns​ 

table_from_columns(columns: dict) -> Table

A table made from a dictionary from column names to lists of values (one for each row), for when you have the data column by column. 

table_from_columns({
    "name": ["Ada", "Grace", "Alan"],
    "born": [1815, 1906, 1912],
})
name born
Ada 1815
Grace 1906
Alan 1912

load_table​ 

load_table(source: str) -> Table

A table read from a CSV ("comma separated values") file: either a file in the same folder as your program (when source is a file name, like "voters.csv"), or one on the web (when source starts with https://). The first line of the CSV gives the names of the columns. 

recipes_raw = load_table("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/neu-pdi/cs2000-public-resources/refs/heads/main/static/support/5-recipes.csv")
recipes_raw.head(3)
title servings prep time
Classic Pancakes 4 15
Banana Oatmeal Muffins 12 20
Avocado Toast 2 10

Every value loaded from a CSV is a string, including the ones that look like numbers, and an empty cell is the empty string "": 

recipes_raw.row(0)
{'title': 'Classic Pancakes', 'servings': '4', 'prep time': '15'}

To convert a column of numbers, use transform_column with int (for whole numbers) or float: 

recipes = recipes_raw.transform_column("servings", int).transform_column("prep time", int)
recipes.row(0)
{'title': 'Classic Pancakes', 'servings': 4, 'prep time': 15}

If some values in a column aren't numbers (e.g., "", or "1,234"), int and float cause an error that names the row, so you'll need to write a function that handles those values, and use that with transform_column instead.

A CSV saved by Excel loads either way it can be saved ("CSV UTF-8", or a plain "CSV"). An address that gives back a web page rather than a CSV, such as a file's page on GitHub, is said to be one, with the fix (use the address of its Raw button). A file next to your program can be up to 50 MB. In the browser, an address on the web only works if its site allows other sites to read it: if load_table reports that it could not reach an address, download the CSV, add it to your repository (next to your program), and load it by its file name instead.

Getting information from tables​

columns​ 

t.columns() -> list[str]

The names of the table's columns, in order. 

workouts.columns()
['date', 'activity', 'duration']

length​ 

t.length() -> int

The number of rows in the table. (len(t) gives the same thing.) 

workouts.length()
5

row​ 

t.row(n: int) -> dict

Row number n of the table, as a dict from column names to values. The first row is number 0, and the last is one less than the number of rows. 

workouts.row(1)
{'date': '2025-04-02', 'activity': 'Yoga', 'duration': 45}
workouts.row(5)
IndexError: there is no row 5: this table's rows are numbered 0 to 4.

To get one value from a row, write the column's name in square brackets after it: 

workouts.row(1)["activity"]
'Yoga'
workouts.row(1)["time"]
KeyError: this row has no column "time" (it has: date, activity, duration).

column​ 

t.column(name: str) -> list

All of the values in a column, as a list, in order. 

workouts.column("duration")
[30, 45, 60, 25, 50]

rows​ 

t.rows() -> list[dict]

All of the rows, as a list of dicts. 

workouts.rows()
[{'date': '2025-04-01', 'activity': 'Running', 'duration': 30},
 {'date': '2025-04-02', 'activity': 'Yoga', 'duration': 45},
 {'date': '2025-04-03', 'activity': 'Cycling', 'duration': 60},
 {'date': '2025-04-04', 'activity': 'Running', 'duration': 25},
 {'date': '2025-04-05', 'activity': 'Yoga', 'duration': 50}]

Making new tables​

filter​ 

t.filter(keep: function) -> Table

A table with only the rows for which keep(row) returns True. Note that we give filter the function itself (with no parentheses after its name): filter calls it on each row. 

def is_long(r: dict) -> bool:
    """whether the workout lasted at least 45 minutes"""
    return r["duration"] >= 45

workouts.filter(is_long)
date activity duration
2025-04-02 Yoga 45
2025-04-03 Cycling 60
2025-04-05 Yoga 50 
workouts.filter(lambda r: r["activity"] == "Yoga")
date activity duration
2025-04-02 Yoga 45
2025-04-05 Yoga 50

transform_column​ 

t.transform_column(name: str, change: function) -> Table

A table where every value v in the column name is replaced by change(v). 

workouts.transform_column("duration", lambda minutes: minutes / 60)
date activity duration
2025-04-01 Running 0.5
2025-04-02 Yoga 0.75
2025-04-03 Cycling 1.0
2025-04-04 Running 0.4166666666666667
2025-04-05 Yoga 0.8333333333333334 
workouts.transform_column("activity", lambda a: a.upper())
date activity duration
2025-04-01 RUNNING 30
2025-04-02 YOGA 45
2025-04-03 CYCLING 60
2025-04-04 RUNNING 25
2025-04-05 YOGA 50

add_column​ 

t.add_column(name: str, compute: function) -> Table
t.add_column(name: str, values: list) -> Table

A table with a new column, at the right, called name. Its value in each row is either compute(row), or, if given a list, the values in the list (one for each row, in order). 

def calories(r: dict) -> float:
    """estimated calories burned in the workout"""
    return r["duration"] * 8

workouts.add_column("calories", calories)
date activity duration calories
2025-04-01 Running 30 240
2025-04-02 Yoga 45 360
2025-04-03 Cycling 60 480
2025-04-04 Running 25 200
2025-04-05 Yoga 50 400 
workouts.add_column("rating", [4, 5, 3, 4, 5])
date activity duration rating
2025-04-01 Running 30 4
2025-04-02 Yoga 45 5
2025-04-03 Cycling 60 3
2025-04-04 Running 25 4
2025-04-05 Yoga 50 5

add_row​ 

t.add_row(row: list | dict) -> Table

A table with one more row, at the end: either a list with one value for each column, in order, or a dict from column names to values. 

workouts.add_row(["2025-04-06", "Swimming", 40])
date activity duration
2025-04-01 Running 30
2025-04-02 Yoga 45
2025-04-03 Cycling 60
2025-04-04 Running 25
2025-04-05 Yoga 50
2025-04-06 Swimming 40 
workouts.add_row({"date": "2025-04-06", "activity": "Swimming", "duration": 40})
date activity duration
2025-04-01 Running 30
2025-04-02 Yoga 45
2025-04-03 Cycling 60
2025-04-04 Running 25
2025-04-05 Yoga 50
2025-04-06 Swimming 40

select_columns​ 

t.select_columns(names: list[str]) -> Table

A table with only the columns in names, in that order. 

workouts.select_columns(["activity", "date"])
activity date
Running 2025-04-01
Yoga 2025-04-02
Cycling 2025-04-03
Running 2025-04-04
Yoga 2025-04-05

order_by​ 

t.order_by(name: str, ascending: bool = True) -> Table

A table with the same rows, sorted by the column name: smallest first if ascending is True (or left out), and largest first if it is False. Strings are sorted in dictionary order (with all uppercase letters before all lowercase ones). 

workouts.order_by("duration", ascending=True)
date activity duration
2025-04-04 Running 25
2025-04-01 Running 30
2025-04-02 Yoga 45
2025-04-05 Yoga 50
2025-04-03 Cycling 60 
workouts.order_by("activity", ascending=False)
date activity duration
2025-04-02 Yoga 45
2025-04-05 Yoga 50
2025-04-01 Running 30
2025-04-04 Running 25
2025-04-03 Cycling 60

head and tail​ 

t.head(n: int = 10) -> Table
t.tail(n: int = 10) -> Table

A table of just the first (head) or last (tail) n rows: 10, if n is left out. 

workouts.head(2)
date activity duration
2025-04-01 Running 30
2025-04-02 Yoga 45 
workouts.tail(2)
date activity duration
2025-04-04 Running 25
2025-04-05 Yoga 50

Summarizing columns​

sum, mean, min, and max​ 

t.sum(name: str) -> int | float
t.mean(name: str) -> float
t.min(name: str)
t.max(name: str)

The total, average, smallest value, and largest value of a column. sum and mean need a column of numbers (the sum of whole numbers is a whole number); min and max also work on strings (dictionary order). At #level beginner and #level intermediate, True and False are not numbers to a table: sum, mean and the charts refuse them.

min, max and order_by refuse a column of numbers that is still text, when comparing it as text would give a different answer (as text, "9" comes after "100"), and say to convert it first: 

recipes_raw.max("servings")
TypeError: max compares column "servings" as text, and as text "12" comes before "2": the values were read from a CSV and never converted to numbers. Convert the column first: transform_column("servings", int).
workouts.sum("duration")
210
workouts.mean("duration")
42.0
workouts.min("duration")
25
workouts.max("activity")
'Yoga'

For anything else, like the median or the standard deviation, use a column (a list) with Python's own statistics library: 

import statistics

statistics.median(workouts.column("duration"))
45
statistics.stdev(workouts.column("duration"))
14.404860290887934

Comparing tables​

Two tables are == when they have the same columns, in the same order, holding the same values, in the same order: 

workouts.head(2) == table(
    ["date", "activity", "duration"],
    [
        ["2025-04-01", "Running", 30],
        ["2025-04-02", "Yoga", 45],
    ],
)
True
workouts.head(2) == workouts.tail(2)
False

So you can test a function that produces a table by comparing its result with the table you expect: 

def long_workouts(t: Table) -> Table:
    """the workouts of at least 45 minutes"""
    return t.filter(is_long)

def test_long_workouts():
    assert long_workouts(workouts.head(3)) == table(
        ["date", "activity", "duration"],
        [
            ["2025-04-02", "Yoga", 45],
            ["2025-04-03", "Cycling", 60],
        ],
    )

When a test like this fails, PLL says where the two tables differ: the first row that does, or the columns, or the number of rows.

Charts​

Charts are made by methods on tables, and produce images, which show up in the interactions panel. Since a chart is an image, beside, above and the rest work on it, and a function that returns one is annotated -> Image. Every chart can also be given a title=, and needs a table with at least one row. The examples use this table: 

study = table(
    ["name", "year", "hours", "score"],
    [
        ["Avery", "first", 2, 62],
        ["Blake", "second", 4, 71],
        ["Casey", "first", 5, 74],
        ["Devon", "third", 7, 80],
        ["Emery", "second", 8, 85],
        ["Finley", "first", 3, 68],
        ["Gray", "third", 10, 91],
        ["Harper", "second", 6, 79],
    ],
)
study
name year hours score
Avery first 2 62
Blake second 4 71
Casey first 5 74
Devon third 7 80
Emery second 8 85
Finley first 3 68
Gray third 10 91
Harper second 6 79

bar_chart​ 

t.bar_chart(labels: str, values: str) -> Image

One bar per row, labeled with the row's value in the labels column, and as tall as its value in the values column. 

study.bar_chart("name", "score")

freq_bar_chart​ 

t.freq_bar_chart(name: str) -> Image

One bar for each different value in the column name, as tall as the number of rows that have that value. 

study.freq_bar_chart("year")

pie_chart​ 

t.pie_chart(labels: str, values: str) -> Image

One slice per row, labeled with the row's value in the labels column, and sized by its share of the total of the values column. 

study.pie_chart("name", "hours", title="Hours studied")

histogram​ 

t.histogram(name: str, bins: int = 10, bin_width: float = None) -> Image

How many rows have values in each range (or bin) of the column name. Give it bins= to choose how many bins there are, or bin_width= to choose how wide each one is (a histogram can have at most 1,000 bins). 

study.histogram("score", bin_width=5)

study.histogram("score", bins=3)

scatter_plot​ 

t.scatter_plot(x: str, y: str) -> Image

One point per row, at its values in the x and y columns. 

study.scatter_plot("hours", "score")

line_chart​ 

t.line_chart(x: str, y: str) -> Image

The same points as scatter_plot, joined by lines, in order of x. 

study.line_chart("hours", "score")

dot_plot​ 

t.dot_plot(name: str) -> Image

One dot per row, along the values of the column name, stacked where rows share a value. 

study.dot_plot("hours")

box_plot​ 

t.box_plot(name: str) -> Image

A box and whisker plot of the column name: its quartiles, range, and any outliers. 

study.box_plot("score")

lr_plot​ 

t.lr_plot(x: str, y: str) -> Image

A scatter plot, with the line that best fits the points (a linear regression), and how well it fits (r²) in the title. 

study.lr_plot("hours", "score")

Labeled plots​ 

t.labeled_scatter_plot(labels: str, x: str, y: str) -> Image
t.labeled_dot_plot(labels: str, name: str) -> Image
t.labeled_lr_plot(labels: str, x: str, y: str) -> Image

Like scatter_plot, dot_plot, and lr_plot, but with each point colored by its value in the labels column, with a key. 

study.labeled_scatter_plot("year", "hours", "score")

linear_regression​ 

t.linear_regression(x: str, y: str) -> tuple[float, float, float]

The line of best fit (the one lr_plot draws) as numbers instead of a picture: a tuple of its slope, its intercept, and r². 

study.linear_regression("hours", "score")
(3.5037593984962405, 56.54135338345865, 0.9883485954595933)

function_plot​ 

function_plot(f: function, x_min: float, x_max: float) -> Image

A plot of the function f, for x from x_min to x_max. (It isn't a method: it doesn't need a table.) 

function_plot(lambda x: x * x, -3, 3)

Using pandas​

Later in the semester, we'll learn pandas, a widely used Python library for working with tables. t.to_pandas() turns a PLL table into a pandas DataFrame: 

workouts.to_pandas()
         date activity  duration
0  2025-04-01  Running        30
1  2025-04-02     Yoga        45
2  2025-04-03  Cycling        60
3  2025-04-04  Running        25
4  2025-04-05     Yoga        50

Charts with matplotlib​

matplotlib, the most widely used Python library for charts, works too: plt.show() shows each figure in the interactions panel, as a picture. 

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.plot([1, 2, 3, 4], [1, 4, 9, 16])
plt.title("Squares")
plt.show()

Any other package that Pyodide (the Python PLL runs on) has can be imported too: numpy, scipy, requests, and many more. The first time, it is downloaded, which needs the network.
